What is the formula for the price in terms of the other variables?"] ["question-220b7284-89df-58d8-b7fb-14c6a632a4f4" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate $P,$ so we will treat the other variables $E,$ $Q,$ and $C$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $P.$

First, we add $C$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}E & =PQ-C \\ E+C & =PQ-C+C \\ E+C & =PQ\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $Q$ to get $P$ alone:

$$
\begin{aligned}E+C & =PQ \\ \frac{E+C}{Q} & =\frac{PQ}{Q} \\ \frac{E+C}{Q} & =P\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $P=\frac{E+C}{Q}.$

**Note:** This result assumes that $Q\ne 0.$"] ["question-220b7284-89df-58d8-b7fb-14c6a632a4f4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-7599f77d-da1f-5c75-baeb-b3ad971719bd" "answer-field-7599f77d-da1f-5c75-baeb-b3ad971719bd"] [17592186064195 :knowledge-point/questions "question-220b7284-89df-58d8-b7fb-14c6a632a4f4"] [17592186065434 :tutorial/content "Sometimes we might be given an equation that contains more than one variable and asked to isolate one of the variables. This means that we need to put the variable we're interested in on one side of the equation (on its own) and everything else on the other.

For example, suppose we want to isolate $n$ in the equation

$$
2n - k = q + 5k.
$$

The equation has three variables, $n,$ $k,$ and $q.$ However, we will treat the variables $k$ and $q$ as constants because we are solving for $n$ only. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $n\mathbin{.}$ 

First, we add $k$ to both sides:

$$
\eqalign{
		2n - k &= q + 5k \[5pt]
		2n - k + k &= q + 5k +k \[5pt]
		2n &= q + 6k \
	}
$$

 

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		2n &= q + 6k \[5pt]
		\dfrac {2n} {2} &= \dfrac {q+6k} {2} \
n &= \dfrac {q+6k} {2}
	}
$$

 

Because the equation is now solved for $n$, we say that we've made $n$ **the subject** of the equation."] [17592186064443 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] [17592186134243 :question/problem "Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

["question-86358ef9-78e9-5caa-a7a3-a7c614e96d69" :question/problem "Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["question-86358ef9-78e9-5caa-a7a3-a7c614e96d69" :question/worked-solution "First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}15 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}15 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-86358ef9-78e9-5caa-a7a3-a7c614e96d69" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-5ae069ad-82b0-5089-9f78-df2bcd3c3331" :answer-field/id #uuid The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

["question-5208d74a-f4b7-5436-9bf1-918aa4bcaa25" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $4x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $2\sqrt{3}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\sqrt{2}\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest."] ["question-5208d74a-f4b7-5436-9bf1-918aa4bcaa25" :question/worked-solution "![](images/01/017463f3ac8abac9c2b00c4d9a715a4109a5f4bc1b070e0a12c4d3a7bac64351.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{3}\,m/s$ when $x=2\sqrt{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{3})^{2} & =2(2\sqrt{2})^{2}+C \\ C & =6-16 \\ C & =-10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{x}^{2}-10.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}-10 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =2{x}^{2}-10 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =10 \\ {x}^{2} & =5 \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{5}\,m\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-5208d74a-f4b7-5436-9bf1-918aa4bcaa25" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-748a88b6-3bf6-5b57-aacf-5ce371f8acba" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(2x-3)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $2\,m/s$ when its displacement is $3\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest."] ["question-bf4a1221-96ce-539b-bfe1-3711516162e7" :question/worked-solution "![](images/ca/ca6267f534b9cad9bc1646eef473d85aab1ba6a5f4738b8212b107b753ea2381.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x-3)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2x-3.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2x-3.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (2x-3)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{2}-3x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=3\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-3x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =(3)^{2}-3(3)+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{2}-3x+2.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-3x+2 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-3x+2 \\ {x}^{2}-3x+2 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =1\,m,\,2\,m.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-bf4a1221-96ce-539b-bfe1-3711516162e7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c6154e74-64bf-5093-bf56-6eed3e0fc3f3" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(3+kx)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=8\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=8\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $8\,m,$ find the value of $k.$"] ["question-f72c0da0-a5f4-5e3b-8c36-5827ed531170" :question/worked-solution "![](images/f3/f368d2de12462a1790322edca188232bf8fafe3951facdb29b334e285807b9fe.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(3+kx)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=3+kx.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=3+kx.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (3+kx)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=3x+\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =3x+\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =3(0)+\frac{k(0)^{2}}{2}+C \\ C & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=3x+\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+32.
$$

Finally, since $v=8\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when $x=8\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =3x+\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+32 \\ \frac{1}{2}(8\sqrt{2})^{2} & =3(8)+\frac{k(8)^{2}}{2}+32 \\ 64 & =24+32k+32 \\ 32k & =8 \\ k & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f72c0da0-a5f4-5e3b-8c36-5827ed531170" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-6c0cd56a-fac1-59c9-9082-8dcbbdf2dead" :answer-field/id #uuid When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of the acceleration is $k{x}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant, and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=8\sqrt{17}\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has a velocity of $v=8\,m/s$ when its displacement is $4\,m,$ find the value of $k.$"] ["question-e3dde6ce-080b-590e-80f0-4c60a929946f" :question/worked-solution "![](images/f3/f3879ccc6084d9a0ef8bef2e211e2e7fd9dcc811fb04f06c2ef7429e4d574871.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $k{x}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-k{x}^{3}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-k{x}^{3}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-k{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-\frac{k}{4}{x}^{4}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=8\sqrt{17}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-\frac{k}{4}{x}^{4}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(8\sqrt{17})^{2} & =-\frac{k}{4}(0)^{4}+C \\ C & =544\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=544-\frac{k}{4}{x}^{4}.
$$

Finally, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=4\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =544-\frac{k}{4}{x}^{4} \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =544-\frac{k}{4}(4)^{4} \\ 32 & =544-64k \\ 64k & =512 \\ k & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e3dde6ce-080b-590e-80f0-4c60a929946f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-efd9e216-e266-5141-b8bb-3d95bb41fe42" :answer-field/id #uuid acceleration is $k\sqrt[3]{x}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=8\,m/s$ when its displacement is $8\,m,$ find the value of $k.$"] ["question-2593d620-c288-5ff9-965a-23a30b035fd9" :question/worked-solution "![](images/77/771929267e75b5d45b9777399c784fafc570386834eee6738fead9ff1bb78e5e.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k\sqrt[3]{x}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k\sqrt[3]{x}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k\sqrt[3]{x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k\sqrt[3]{x}\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{3k}{4}{x}^{4/3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{3k}{4}{x}^{4/3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =\frac{3k}{4}(0)^{4/3}+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{3k}{4}{x}^{4/3}+2.
$$

Finally, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=8\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{3k}{4}{x}^{4/3}+2 \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =\frac{3k}{4}(8)^{4/3}+2 \\ 32 & =12k+2 \\ 12k & =30 \\ k & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2593d620-c288-5ff9-965a-23a30b035fd9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c645bc4d-e925-5887-895a-ddac573c52dd" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(7-x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle."] ["question-5fda4f28-bb84-514e-9e1c-0feb53f5b922" :question/worked-solution "![](images/51/51ccc6e3e341931c7a244c4617ede78f901478487589f9023b16c3dae80ebc62.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(7-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=7-x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}7-x & =0 \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=7\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,7)$ | $7$ | $(7,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $6$ |  | $8$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $1>0$ | $0$ | $-1<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=7\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=7-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (7-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{6})^{2} & =7(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =14x-{x}^{2}+6 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-{x}^{2}+14x+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+14x+6}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(7)=\sqrt{-(7)^{2}+14(7)+6}=\sqrt{55}\,m/s
$$"] ["question-5fda4f28-bb84-514e-9e1c-0feb53f5b922" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-561bb6d9-fdfa-583e-add7-ec5538f0b8c0" :answer-field/id #uuid "answer-field-561bb6d9-fdfa-583e-add7-ec5538f0b8c0"] [17592186179715 :knowledge-point/questions "question-5fda4f28-bb84-514e-9e1c-0feb53f5b922"] [17592186180703 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to calculate a particle's velocity and displacement when its acceleration is a function of *displacement.* In this lesson, we'll use this knowledge to compute various properties of a particle in motion.  

Suppose a particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. Its displacement from the origin is $x\,\rm{m},$ its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ and its acceleration is $2x\,\rm{m/s}^2.$ 

![](images/52/5222b12a7f08a33dc981ac95bd717cce945e1d2e3565fb3631f108fd0f307a12.png)

Furthermore, suppose $P$ has velocity $2\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $\sqrt{3}\,\rm{m}.$ 

Let's use this information to determine at which values of $x$ the particle is instantaneously at rest.

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $2x\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =2x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x
=
\int 2x \:\textrm{d}x
$$

Let's write down what we know:

- $a=100$ is the total number of students initially

- $r=1.6$ is the growth rate ($160%$ expressed as a decimal)

- $t=$ the time (in weeks) after the launch

The formula for exponential growth is

$$
S=a(1+r)^{t}.
$$

Therefore, the correct expression for $S(t)$ is

$$
S=100\cdot (1+1.6)^{t}.
$$

Simplifying the above, we get

$$
S(t)=100\cdot (2.6)^{t}.
$$

To find the total number of students after $3$ weeks, we evaluate the above for $t=3:$

$$
S(3)=100\cdot (2.6)^{3}≈1758
$$

Therefore, the estimated number of students after $3$ weeks is $1758.$"] ["question-0f781a71-78ec-54be-875d-95c07fb380d7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] If the deer population doubles every year, can we find a function that gives the number of deer after $t$ years? 

First, let's write down what we know:

- $a = 120$ is the **initial number** of deer

- $b =2$ is the **growth factor** (equal to $2$ because the number of deer doubles every year)

- $t=$ the time (in years)

We let $y(t)$ be the number of deer in the reserve after $t$ years.  The formula for $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y(t) = ab^t.
$$

Substituting our values for $a$ and $b,$ we get

$$
y(t) = 120\cdot 2^t.
$$

We can use this formula to find the number of deer in the reserve for any value of $t \geq 0.$ For example, to find the number of deer after $3$ years, we substitute $t=3$ into the function:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(3) & =120\cdot {2}^{3} \\  & =120\cdot 8 \\  & =960\end{aligned}
$$

So there will be $960$ deer after $3$ years.

Finally, notice that substituting $t=0$ into the formula gives the initial number of deer:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =120\cdot {2}^{0} \\  & =120\cdot 1 \\  & =120\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186148683 :tutorial/content "When dealing with exponential growth, it's more common to be given a **growth rate** instead of a growth factor. A growth rate is usually expressed as a percent.

For example, suppose that an investor invests $\[math]500$ dollars in the shares of some high-growth companies. It's expected that the investment will grow by $35\%$ each year. Can we write a function that describes the value of the investment after $t$ years? 

Let's write down what we know:

- $a=\[/math]500$ is the **initial value** of the investment

- $r = 0.35$ is the **growth rate** (this is simply $35\%$ expressed as a decimal)

- $t$ is the time (in years)

Let $y(t)$ be the value of the investment after $t$ years. The formula for $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y = a(1+r)^t.
$$

Substituting in our values for $a$ and $r,$ we get

$$
y(t) = 500(1+0.35)^t.
$$

Simplifying the above, we arrive at

$$
y(t) = 500(1.35)^t.
$$

When creating exponential growth functions, the key takeaway is this:

- If you're given a **growth rate** $r$ (usually expressed as a percent), then use the formula $y = a(1+r)^t.$

- If you're given a **growth factor** $b,$ then use the formula $y = ab^t.$"] [17592186147671 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-180b64b1-b15e-57ee-9a92-ff79a509bb19" :question/id #uuid "180b64b1-b15e-57ee-9a92-ff79a509bb19"] ["question-180b64b1-b15e-57ee-9a92-ff79a509bb19" :question/math-academy-id "q-129431"] ["question-180b64b1-b15e-57ee-9a92-ff79a509bb19" :question/problem "$\sqrt{{a}^{2}{b}^{2}}=$"] ["question-180b64b1-b15e-57ee-9a92-ff79a509bb19" :question/worked-solution "Remember that the square root of a perfect square can be simplified using absolute value.

$$
\sqrt{{x}^{2}}=|x|
$$

Also, we notice that ${a}^{2}$ and ${b}^{2}$ are perfect squares.

First, we write the expression under the square root as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{a}^{2}{b}^{2}} & =\sqrt{a\cdot a\cdot b\cdot b} \\  & =\sqrt{a\cdot b\cdot a\cdot b} \\  & =\sqrt{(ab)\cdot (ab)} \\  & =\sqrt{(ab)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we take the absolute value of the squared quantity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{(ab)^{2}} & =|ab|\end{aligned}

How many square kilometers does the area increase by between day $1$ and day $2?$"] ["question-38bb781d-e24d-5ca2-821e-7901089bd6a3" :question/worked-solution "To find the growth of the patch between day $1$ and day $2$, we need to subtract the area after day $1$ from the area after day $2.$ So we need to calculate

$$
A(2)-A(1).
$$

First, we find the area after the first day, $A(1)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}A(1) & =10\cdot (1.1)^{1} \\  & =10\cdot 1.1 \\  & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find $A(2),$ the area after the second day:

$$
\begin{aligned}A(2) & =10\cdot (1.1)^{2} \\  & =10\cdot 1.21 \\  & =12.1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the growth of the patch between day $1$ and day $2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A(2)-A(1) & =12.1-11=1.1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the area increased by $1.1$ square kilometer between day $1$ and day $2.$"] ["question-38bb781d-e24d-5ca2-821e-7901089bd6a3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] is given by $M(t)=1\,000\cdot (1.6)^{t}$, where $t$ is the time in years since the beginning of the observations. How many additional rodents will be born in the colony between years $2$ and $3?$"] ["question-978bca7b-e158-5bd2-ae01-fa65d0556739" :question/worked-solution "To find the growth in the population of rodents between year $2$ and year $3$, we need to subtract the population after year $2$ from the population after year $3.$ So we need to calculate

$$
M(3)-M(2).
$$

First, we find the population after the second year, $M(2)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}M(2) & =1\,000\cdot (1.6)^{(2)} \\  & =1\,000\cdot 2.56 \\  & =2\,560\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find $M(3),$ the population after the third year:

$$
\begin{aligned}M(3) & =1\,000\cdot (1.6)^{(3)} \\  & =1\,000\cdot 4.096 \\  & =4\,096\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the growth in the population between year $2$ and year $3$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}M(3)-M(2) & =4\,096-2\,560=1\,536.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the population of rodents increased by $1\,536$ between years $2$ and $3.$"] ["question-978bca7b-e158-5bd2-ae01-fa65d0556739" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] :question/problem "The total area, in square meters,  covered by blueberry bushes in a forest can be modeled by the expression $800\cdot (1.1)^{t},$ where $t$ is the number of years since the year $2015.$ What does the base of the exponential expression $(1.1)$ mean in this context?"] ["question-065bbf88-3b11-5079-b0c1-f463dc0506a1" :question/worked-solution "The answer choices require interpretation as a percent, and so we use the growth rate formula.

The given expression is an exponential growth expression of the form $y(t)=a\cdot (1+r)^{t}$, where:

- $a=800$ represents the initial area covered by the  blueberry bushes

- $1+r=1.1,$ where $r$ is the growth rate

- $t$ is the number of years since $2015$

Solving for $r$:

$$
1+r=1.1\,⟹\,r=0.1
$$

Now, $0.1$ (expressed as a percent) is equal to $10%.$ Therefore, the area covered by the bushes grows at a rate of $10%$ per year."] ["question-065bbf88-3b11-5079-b0c1-f463dc0506a1" If $A$ is a finite set, the supremum of $A$ equals its maximum. 

First, let's write down all the terms of our set by substituting $n=1,2,3,4$ into the expression for the elements of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(-1)^{1}}{(1)^{2}+1} & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{(-1)^{2}}{(2)^{2}+1} & =\frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{(-1)^{3}}{(3)^{2}+1} & =-\frac{1}{10} \\ \frac{(-1)^{4}}{(4)^{2}+1} & =\frac{1}{17}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
A=\{-\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{1}{5},\,-\frac{1}{10},\,\frac{1}{17}\}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}sup(A) & =max\{-\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{1}{5},\,-\frac{1}{10},\,\frac{1}{17}\}=\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186162529 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-d8929061-a36b-574c-a4a0-2a9230b65f4c" :answer/id #uuid "d8929061-a36b-574c-a4a0-2a9230b65f4c"] ["answer-d8929061-a36b-574c-a4a0-2a9230b65f4c" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-d8929061-a36b-574c-a4a0-2a9230b65f4c" :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}"] [17592186160501 :answer-field/correct "answer-d8929061-a36b-574c-a4a0-2a9230b65f4c"] [17592186160501 :answer-field/choices "answer-d8929061-a36b-574c-a4a0-2a9230b65f4c"] [17592186162525 :question/problem "What is the infimum of the set $A=\{0,\,3,\,6,\,9\}?$

For this set, we have {{field-1}}."] ["question-03070e45-f0e3-5991-b98c-709745709961" :question/worked-solution "The supremum of a set $A$ is the smallest upper bound of $A.$

To find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

The elements of $A$ are all the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=7-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{n},\,n\in N=\{1,2,3,4,…\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](images/ca/cae6f56db55b49b98df6ce7e3ae0777e725af14de9dedb5b61b54039bac41860.png)

We see that ${a}_{n}$ is increasing and converges to $7.$ 

So, in our case, we have that

- any number in the set $x\ge 7$ is an upper bound of $A,$

- any number in the set $x<7$ is **not** an upper bound of $A.$ In other words, we can always find a sufficiently large $n$ so that $7-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{n}$ is greater than $x$ for any $x<7.$

Therefore, $[7,\infty )$ is the set of upper bounds of $A,$ and 

$$
sup(A)=min[7,\infty )=7.
$$

Notice that $7$ is *not* the maximum of $A$ (the set $A$ has no maximum). Therefore, we conclude that

$$
sup(A)=7\notin A.
$$"] ["question-03070e45-f0e3-5991-b98c-709745709961" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-11588f66-7282-571e-8e23-97b1f1c241fa" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

What is the supremum of the function $y=f(x)$ shown above?

{{field-1}}"] ["question-fd9f0c45-62d6-5bab-b897-93c9f4793a8e" :question/worked-solution "The supremum of a function is the supremum of the range of the function.

In this case, the range of $f$ is $A=(-1,4].$

To find the supremum of a set $A,$ we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $y\ge 4$ is an upper bound of $A,$

- any number $y<4$ cannot be an upper bound of $A$ because $4,$ an element of $A,$ is greater than $y.$

Therefore, $[4,\infty )$ is the set of upper bounds of $A,$ and

$$
{sup}_{x\in R}f(x)=sup(A)=min[4,\infty )=4.
$$"] ["question-fd9f0c45-62d6-5bab-b897-93c9f4793a8e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-60ad18e2-13e5-50fe-b40b-8175f7273995" :answer-field/id #uuid "60ad18e2-13e5-50fe-b40b-8175f7273995"] ["answer-5b8257c3-cb89-57e7-af23-191b90a42228" :answer/id #uuid "5b8257c3-cb89-57e7-af23-191b90a42228"] ["answer-5b8257c3-cb89-57e7-af23-191b90a42228" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-5b8257c3-cb89-57e7-af23-191b90a42228" :answer/value "4"] ["answer-field-60ad18e2-13e5-50fe-b40b-8175f7273995" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-60ad18e2-13e5-50fe-b40b-8175f7273995" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-60ad18e2-13e5-50fe-b40b-8175f7273995" :answer-field/correct "answer-5b8257c3-cb89-57e7-af23-191b90a42228"] ["answer-field-60ad18e2-13e5-50fe-b40b-8175f7273995" :answer-field/choices "answer-5b8257c3-cb89-57e7-af23-191b90a42228"] ["question-fd9f0c45-62d6-5bab-b897-93c9f4793a8e" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-60ad18e2-13e5-50fe-b40b-8175f7273995"] [17592186162159 :knowledge-point/questions "question-fd9f0c45-62d6-5bab-b897-93c9f4793a8e"] ["question-42308119-ffcd-55c6-b052-68e017e7cc90" :question/id #uuid "42308119-ffcd-55c6-b052-68e017e7cc90"] ["question-42308119-ffcd-55c6-b052-68e017e7cc90" :question/math-academy-id "q-253897"] ["question-42308119-ffcd-55c6-b052-68e017e7cc90" :question/problem "![](images/64/64131e649a82e06d2750d53bdf05b1701b0674a05b70149081ddb58d700adb54.png)

{{field-1}}"] ["question-42308119-ffcd-55c6-b052-68e017e7cc90" :question/worked-solution "The supremum of a function is the supremum of the range of the function.

For this, we can use synthetic division.

We start by drawing up our synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ 3 & 6 & 5 \\  & ↓ & 18 \\  & 6 & 23\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{6x+5}{x-3}=6+\frac{23}{x-3}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{6x+5}{x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int (6+\frac{23}{x-3})\text{d}x \\  & =6\int \text{d}x+23\int \frac{1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6x+23\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-338fe155-640c-56d4-b9a0-1883a5de5f4f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-06e29f29-fb54-5de8-b11c-95711b29f9f5" :answer-field/id #uuid |  | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $-2$ | $6$ | $5$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-12$ |
|  | $6$ | $-7$ |

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{6x+5}{x+2}=6-\frac{7}{x+2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{6x+5}{x+2}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(6-\frac{7}{x+2})\text{d}x \\  & =6{\int }_{1}^{3}\text{d}x-7{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6x{|}_{1}^{3}-7\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|{|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =6(3-1)-7(\operatorname{ln}⁡|3+2|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+2|) \\  & =12-7(\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡3) \\  & =12-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(\,\frac{5}{3}\,).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-660f8bdc-c1bb-5f91-9301-9db16573b0bc" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-8ed473a7-2cf4-592b-b794-efbb9e644086" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{2{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+2x-1}{x-1}=2{x}^{2}-x+1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+2x-1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{2}-x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}x \\  & =2\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{0}^{1}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{1}+x{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2[\frac{{1}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}]-[\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}]+[1-0] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}

["question-8c284bd6-ffb5-522e-9bbf-08c92df09daa" :question/math-academy-id "q-347424"] ["question-8c284bd6-ffb5-522e-9bbf-08c92df09daa" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral:

${\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{7x-2}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}} $-\,\frac{13}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡($
{{field-2}} $)$"] ["question-8c284bd6-ffb5-522e-9bbf-08c92df09daa" :question/worked-solution "First, we pull out the factor of $3$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{7x-2}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{7x-2}{3(x+1/3)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{7x-2}{(x+1/3)}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

|  | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{1}{3}$ | $7$ | $-2$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-\frac{7}{3}$ |
|  | $7$ | $-\frac{13}{3}$ |

So, from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7x-2}{(x+1/3)} & =7-\frac{(13/3)}{(x+1/3)} \\  & =7-\frac{13}{3x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

"question-ae6c8955-529c-5030-96d7-68d6213f0d1e"] [17592186065438 :tutorial/content "How do we calculate $\displaystyle \int\dfrac{3x+2}{x+2}\,\textrm d x\,?$

We need to write the integrand so that it's something we can integrate. One way to do this is to divide $3x+2$ by $x+2$ using polynomial or synthetic division. We'll use synthetic division because it's faster. 

To rewrite $\dfrac{3x+2}{x+2},$ we complete a synthetic division table.

|  | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}-2$ | $3$ | $2$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $-6$ |
|  | $3$ | $-4$ |

This tells us that $\dfrac{3x+2}{x+2}$ can be decomposed into a quotient and remainder as

$$
\dfrac{3x+2}{x+2}= 3 - \dfrac{4}{x+2}.
$$

Now, we can integrate the function, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x+2}{x+2}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3-\frac{4}{x+2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 3\,\text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+C.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186065096 :step/math-academy-id 630729] [17592186065102 :step/math-academy-id 630730] [17592186065103 :step/math-academy-id 630733] [17592186065113 :step/math-academy-id 630736] [17592186064429 :activity/expected-seconds 1080.0] [17592186326788 :question/problem "Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places."] [17592186394752 :question/problem "Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$"] [17592186394752 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$

$$

 

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

["question-c68f1c1a-c6a6-5448-b77c-02d88ae0390d" :question/problem "Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

I. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=y{x}^{2}-4y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-4x$

II. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=3-5x$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=1$

III. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-2{y}^{3}{e}^{{y}^{2}}$"] ["question-c68f1c1a-c6a6-5448-b77c-02d88ae0390d" :question/worked-solution "Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{x}^{2}-4y)={x}^{2}-4 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-4x)={x}^{2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3-5x)=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =0+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-2{y}^{3}{e}^{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y-0 \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and II only'."] ["question-c68f1c1a-c6a6-5448-b77c-02d88ae0390d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] Also, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6x\,\, & \le \,\,-7 \\ \frac{-6x}{-6}\,\, & \ge \,\,\frac{-7}{-6} \\ \frac{-6x}{-6}\,\, & \ge \,\,\frac{7}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $-6$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$

Therefore, the solution is $x \geq \dfrac{7}{6}.$"] [17592186054401 :question/problem "Solve the inequality $-\dfrac{y}{8} \leq -4.$"] [17592186054401 :question/worked-solution "The variable $y$ is being *divided* by $8.$ To isolate $y$ and remove the negative sign, we *multiply* by $-8.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{y}{8}\,\, & \le \,\,-4 \\ (-8)\cdot (-\frac{y}{8})\,\, & \ge \,\,(-8)\cdot (-4) \\ (-8)\cdot (-\frac{y}{8})\,\, & \ge \,\,32\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-8)\cdot (-\frac{y}{8}) & \ge 32 \\ (\cancel{-}8)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{y}{8}) & \ge 32 \\ 8\cdot \frac{y}{8} & \ge 32\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $8$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}8\cdot \frac{y}{8} & \ge 32 \\ \frac{8y}{8} & \ge 32 \\ \frac{\cancel{8}y}{\cancel{8}} & \ge 32 \\ y & \ge 32\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $y \geq 32.$"] [17592186054402 :question/problem "Solve the inequality $-9 \leq -3z.$"] [17592186054402 :question/worked-solution "The variable $z$ is being *multiplied* by $-3.$ To isolate $z,$ we can perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $-3.$ Remember to perform the same operation on both sides.

Now, we can cancel the common factor $-3$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$

$$

Therefore, the solution is $z \leq 3.$"] ["question-a32936a3-d0e7-5359-880f-a816d9cf59f9" :question/id #uuid "a32936a3-d0e7-5359-880f-a816d9cf59f9"] ["question-a32936a3-d0e7-5359-880f-a816d9cf59f9" :question/math-academy-id "q-153998"] ["question-a32936a3-d0e7-5359-880f-a816d9cf59f9" :question/problem "What is the solution to $6z>-5?$"] ["question-a32936a3-d0e7-5359-880f-a816d9cf59f9" :question/worked-solution "The variable $z$ is being *multiplied* by $6.$ To isolate $z,$ we perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $6.$ Remember to perform the same operation on both sides.

$$
\begin{aligned}6z & >-5 \\ \frac{6z}{6} & >\frac{-5}{6} \\ \frac{6z}{6} & >-\frac{5}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $6$ from the numerator and denominator.

$$

["question-e481e652-2dec-5a50-9597-483a3ddecf5c" :question/worked-solution "The variable $x$ is being *multiplied* by $-5.$ To isolate $x,$ we perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by Also, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5x\,\, & <\,\,10 \\ \frac{-5x}{-5}\,\, & >\,\,\frac{10}{-5} \\ \frac{-5x}{-5}\,\, & >\,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $-5$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-5x}{-5} & >-2 \\ \frac{\cancel{-5}x}{\cancel{-5}} & >-2 \\ x & >-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x>-2.$"] ["question-e481e652-2dec-5a50-9597-483a3ddecf5c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-bb6518e0-b1be-56b3-b252-cbc313544571" Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{y}{3}\,\, & \le \,\,4 \\ (-3)\cdot (-\frac{y}{3})\,\, & \ge \,\,(-3)\cdot 4 \\ (-3)\cdot (-\frac{y}{3})\,\, & \ge \,\,-12\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)\cdot (-\frac{y}{3})\,\, & \ge -12 \\ (\cancel{-}3)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{y}{3}) & \ge -12 \\ 3\cdot \frac{y}{3} & \ge -12\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $3$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot \frac{y}{3} & \ge -12 \\ \frac{3y}{3} & \ge -12 \\ \frac{\cancel{3}y}{\cancel{3}} & \ge -12 \\ y & \ge -12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $y\ge -12.$"] ["question-24cf9a94-daed-5188-bbde-60124c7a3e18" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-9febe4e4-9bba-517f-959d-bd5f66e0861c" "question-1c83e356-5c28-5a7c-9e2e-dbd984ca824b"] [17592186055023 :question/problem "Solve the inequality $9\ge -\frac{x}{4}.$"] [17592186055023 :question/worked-solution "The variable $x$ is being *divided* by $4.$ To isolate $x$ and remove the negative sign, we *multiply* by $-4$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}9\,\, & \ge \,\,-\frac{x}{4} \\ (-4)\cdot 9\,\, & \le \,\,(-4)\cdot (-\frac{x}{4}) \\ -36\,\, & \le \,\,(-4)\cdot (-\frac{x}{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}-36\,\, & \le (-4)\cdot (-\frac{x}{4}) \\ -36 & \le (\cancel{-}4)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{x}{4}) \\ -36 & \le 4\cdot \frac{x}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel the common factor $4$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}-36 & \le 4\cdot \frac{x}{4} \\ -36 & \le \frac{4x}{4} \\ -36 & \le \frac{\cancel{4}x}{\cancel{4}} \\ -36 & \le x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the inequality with the variable on the left-hand side:

$$

*When multiplying or dividing both sides by a **negative number**, we flip the inequality sign.*

When we "flip the inequality sign," we switch the direction of the inequality symbol. For example:

- "$\color{blue}<$" becomes "$\color{red}>$" and vice versa

- "$\color{blue}\leq$" becomes "$\color{red}\geq$" and vice versa

To illustrate, consider the following inequality:

$$
- 3x \gt 9
$$

We can solve this inequality using the multiplication principle. However, when we divide both sides by $-3,$ we have to flip the inequality sign. 

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x\,\, & >\,\,9 \\ \frac{-3x}{-3}\,\, & <\,\,\frac{9}{-3} \\ \frac{-3x}{-3}\,\, & <\,\,-3 \\ \frac{\cancel{-3}x}{\cancel{-3}}\,\, & <\,\,-3 \\ x\,\, & <\,\,-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x \lt -3.$

We reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form to obtain the matrix $U,$ as usual. However, instead of writing zeros below the main diagonal, we will instead write down the entries of the matrix $L.$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+1{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 5 \\ \,\,-1\,\, & 6 & 11\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 5 \\ -1 & \,2\, & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
L=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,U=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, since ${l}_{32}=2$ and ${u}_{33}=1,$ we get

$$
{l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=2\cdot 1=2.
$$"] ["question-9f75fb2d-2340-51fb-8c92-f477a45ff81a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-4e02f7e6-ceb7-5cfc-b631-3a84b30133ca" :answer-field/id #uuid - The range of the branch defined on $x\in [1,4)$ is $\{1\}$

$$
-1<f(x)<3.
$$

["question-fadc73be-dedf-5384-82b7-e3c8b9123466" :question/worked-solution "First, we distribute the $2$ over each of the terms in parentheses.

$$

Then, we collect like terms.

$$
\begin{aligned}12-3x+8x-10 & = \\ (12-10)+(-3x+8x) & = \\ (2)+(5x) & = \\ 2+5x\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-fadc73be-dedf-5384-82b7-e3c8b9123466" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-56cc9ec7-a78c-54b1-a942-1c31a8e69346" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-a5bfe454-c84f-5da8-9381-6959e5f62f7a" :question/problem "Let $L$ be the line in ${R}^{3}$ that passes through the points $(1,-1,2)$ and $(-1,1,1).$ Which of the following statements are I. $L$ contains the zero-vector

II. $L$ is closed under vector addition

III. $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
\frac{x-1}{-2}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-2}{-1}.
$$

But this line does not pass through the origin since 

$$
\frac{(0)-1}{-2}=\frac{(0)+1}{2}\ne \frac{(0)-2}{-1}\,\times 
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider the vectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ from $L$ (the position vectors of the given points). Then,

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

However, the point $(0,0,3)$ does not belong to $L$ since

$$
\frac{(0)-1}{-2}=\frac{(0)+1}{2}\ne -(3)+2.\,\times 
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only.""] ["question-a5bfe454-c84f-5da8-9381-6959e5f62f7a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-af22d48e-5724-584d-b3a5-2b9d70fcf5d0" :question/problem "Let $Π$ be the plane with equation $z=3x+2y$ in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $Π$ contains the zero-vector

II. $Π$ is closed under vector addition

III. $Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $Π$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$"] ["question-00c50921-42ae-53d0-a1bc-1a992257ffe3" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ 3x+2y\end{aligned}],\,x,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $z=3x+2y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =3x+2y \\ (0) & =3(0)+2(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]\in Π$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ 3{b}_{1}+2{b}_{2}\end{aligned}]\in Π.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ 3{b}_{1}+2{b}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ (3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2})+(3{b}_{1}+2{b}_{2})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ 3({a}_{1}+{b}_{1})+2({a}_{2}+{b}_{2})\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=3x+2y.$ Therefore, $a+b\in Π.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]\in Π$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot [\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ k(3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ 3k{a}_{1}+2k{a}_{2}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=3x+2y.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in Π.$

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are true, the plane $Π$ must be a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "All the statements are true.""] ["question-00c50921-42ae-53d0-a1bc-1a992257ffe3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-f7253d28-4651-534c-8fab-305435de6a5d" :question/problem "In an online study, $60%$ of participants reported enjoying painting. Of those, $25%$ said they preferred painting landscapes. What percentage of all participants preferred landscape painting?"] ["question-f7253d28-4651-534c-8fab-305435de6a5d" :question/worked-solution "Let $x$ be the total number of participants.

We're told that $60%$ of participants enjoy painting. Thus, the number of participants who enjoy painting is $0.6x.$

We are also told that of those participants, $25%$ preferred landscapes. So, the number of participants who preferred landscape painting is

$$
0.25(0.6x)=0.15x.
$$

The expression $0.15x$ represents $15%$ of $x.$ Therefore, $15%$ of all participants preferred landscape painting."] ["question-f7253d28-4651-534c-8fab-305435de6a5d" :question/difficulty "Calculate $∇\times (F-G)$ at the point $(-2,0,3)$ for the vector fields $F$ and $G,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=z{e}^{y}\,i+3\,j-x\,k,\,(∇\times G)(x,y,z)=2x{e}^{y}\,i-2{e}^{y}\,j.
$$"] [17592186179911 :question/worked-solution "If $F$ and $G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for curl:

- $∇\times (kF)=k∇\times F$

- $∇\times (F+G)=∇\times F+∇\times G$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (F-G) & =∇\times F-∇\times G.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to calculate $∇\times F.$ In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ z{e}^{y} & 3 & -x\end{aligned}| \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(-x)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(3)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(-x)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(z{e}^{y})]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(3)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(z{e}^{y})]k \\  & =(0-0)i-((-1)-{e}^{y})j+(0-z{e}^{y})k \\  & =({e}^{y}+1)\,j-z{e}^{y}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the linearity properties, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (F-G) & =∇\times F-∇\times G \\  & =({e}^{y}+1)\,j-z{e}^{y}\,k-[2x{e}^{y}\,i-2{e}^{y}\,j] \\  & =({e}^{y}+1)\,j-z{e}^{y}\,k-2x{e}^{y}\,i+2{e}^{y}\,j \\  & =-2x{e}^{y}\,i+(3{e}^{y}+1)\,j-z{e}^{y}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating at the point $(-2,0,3),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\times (F-G))(-2,0,3) & =-2(-2){e}^{0}\,i+(3{e}^{0}+1)\,j-3{e}^{0}\,k \\  & =4\,i+4\,j-3\,k.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186179911 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-08afb4e5-f12f-5c39-8a4d-af1df6ce9745" :answer/id #uuid "08afb4e5-f12f-5c39-8a4d-af1df6ce9745"] ["answer-08afb4e5-f12f-5c39-8a4d-af1df6ce9745" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-08afb4e5-f12f-5c39-8a4d-af1df6ce9745" :answer/value "-2\,i-5\,j+k"] ["answer-5c3feea7-809e-5194-b77d-2a337acc1747" :answer/id #uuid "5c3feea7-809e-5194-b77d-2a337acc1747"] ["answer-5c3feea7-809e-5194-b77d-2a337acc1747" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-5c3feea7-809e-5194-b77d-2a337acc1747" :answer/value "2\,i+3\,k"] ["answer-d2f59412-f61c-5a93-9b03-097a20b5443f" :answer/id #uuid "d2f59412-f61c-5a93-9b03-097a20b5443f"] ["answer-d2f59412-f61c-5a93-9b03-097a20b5443f" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-d2f59412-f61c-5a93-9b03-097a20b5443f" :answer/value "4\,i+4\,j-3\,k"] ["answer-79d18dc1-c0bb-50e7-a72e-25cf91922adb" :answer/id #uuid "79d18dc1-c0bb-50e7-a72e-25cf91922adb"] ["answer-79d18dc1-c0bb-50e7-a72e-25cf91922adb" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-79d18dc1-c0bb-50e7-a72e-25cf91922adb" :answer/value "5\,j-2\,k"] [17592186177135 :answer-field/correct "answer-d2f59412-f61c-5a93-9b03-097a20b5443f"] [17592186177135 :answer-field/choices "answer-08afb4e5-f12f-5c39-8a4d-af1df6ce9745"] [17592186177135 :answer-field/choices "answer-5c3feea7-809e-5194-b77d-2a337acc1747"] [17592186177135 :answer-field/choices "answer-d2f59412-f61c-5a93-9b03-097a20b5443f"] [17592186177135 :answer-field/choices "answer-79d18dc1-c0bb-50e7-a72e-25cf91922adb"] ["question-c8edc0c0-9a3d-5546-8149-aa1e5f0446b7" :question/id #uuid "c8edc0c0-9a3d-5546-8149-aa1e5f0446b7"] ["question-c8edc0c0-9a3d-5546-8149-aa1e5f0446b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-105791"] ["question-c8edc0c0-9a3d-5546-8149-aa1e5f0446b7" :question/problem "Calculate $∇\times (4F+G)$ at the point $(0,1,-1)$ for the vector fields $F$ and $G,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=y{e}^{x}\,i+xz\,j+(y-1)\,\text{k},\,(∇\times G)(x,y,z)=z\,i.
$$"] ["question-c8edc0c0-9a3d-5546-8149-aa1e5f0446b7" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ and $G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for curl:

- $∇\times (kF)=k∇\times F$

- $∇\times (F+G)=∇\times F+∇\times G$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (4F+G) & =∇\times (4F)+∇\times G \\  & =4∇\times F+∇\times G.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to calculate $∇\times F.$ In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ y{e}^{x} & xz & y-1\end{aligned}| \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-1)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xz)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-1)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(y{e}^{x})]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xz)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{x})]k \\  & =(1-x)\,i-(0-0)\,j+(z-{e}^{x})\,k \\  & =(1-x)\,i+(z-{e}^{x})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the linearity properties, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (4F+G) & =4(∇\times F)+∇\times G \\  & =4[(1-x)\,i+(z-{e}^{x})\,k]+z\,i \\  & =4(1-x)\,i+4(z-{e}^{x})\,k+z\,i \\  & =[4(1-x)+z]\,i+4(z-{e}^{x})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating at the point $(0,1,-1),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\times (4F+G))(0,1,-1) & =[4(1-0)+(-1)]\,i+4(-1-{e}^{0})\,k \\  & =[4-1]\,i+4(-1-1)\,k \\  & =3\,i-8\,k.\end{aligned}

$F(x,y,z)=⟨x{e}^{y},z,0⟩$ and the scalar field $f(x,y,z)=x-{e}^{y}.$ Given that

$$
∇\times F=⟨-1,0,-x{e}^{y}⟩,\,∇f=⟨1,-{e}^{y},0⟩,
$$

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(2,0,-3).$"] ["question-f311fcaa-7f7c-50da-9066-652f1bc7fb5e" :question/worked-solution "We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -{e}^{y} & 0 \\ x{e}^{y} & z & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =[-{e}^{y}(0)-0(z)]i-[1(0)-0(x{e}^{y})]j+[1(z)-(-{e}^{y})(x{e}^{y})]k \\  & =0\,i-0\,j+(z+x{e}^{2y})\,k \\  & =⟨0,0,z+x{e}^{2y}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =(x-{e}^{y})⟨-1,0,-x{e}^{y}⟩+⟨0,0,z+x{e}^{2y}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{y}-x,0,x{e}^{2y}-{x}^{2}{e}^{y}⟩+⟨0,0,z+x{e}^{2y}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{y}-x,0,2x{e}^{2y}+z-{x}^{2}{e}^{y}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F)(2,0,-3) & =⟨{e}^{0}-2,0,2(2){e}^{2(0)}+(-3)-(2)^{2}{e}^{0}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f311fcaa-7f7c-50da-9066-652f1bc7fb5e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-87266618-2882-52b8-96d1-51f6b11cd2c6" :answer-field/id #uuid $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,{e}^{3x},2y⟩$ and the scalar field $f(x,y,z)=2x+3.$ Given that

$$
∇\times F=⟨2,0,3{e}^{3x}⟩,\,∇f=⟨2,0,0⟩,
$$

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(0,-1,4).$"] ["question-69db9a7c-5652-51d3-8060-5596c178f982" :question/worked-solution "We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{3x} & 2y\end{aligned}| \\  & =[0(2y)-0({e}^{3x})]i-[2(2y)-0(0)]j+[2({e}^{3x})-0(0)]k \\  & =0\,i-4y\,j+2{e}^{3x}\,k \\  & =⟨0,-4y,2{e}^{3x}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =(2x+3)⟨2,0,3{e}^{3x}⟩+⟨0,-4y,2{e}^{3x}⟩ \\  & =⟨2(2x+3),0,(6x+9){e}^{3x}⟩+⟨0,-4y,2{e}^{3x}⟩ \\  & =⟨2(2x+3),-4y,(6x+11){e}^{3x}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F)(0,-1,4) & =⟨2(2(0)+3),-4(-1),(6(0)+11){e}^{3(0)}⟩ \\  & =⟨6,4,11⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-69db9a7c-5652-51d3-8060-5596c178f982" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-36ec198d-cd51-504c-b007-6c8fdb361499" :answer-field/id #uuid $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\sqrt{x},0⟩$ and the scalar field $f(x,y,z)=-z.$ Given that

$$
∇\times F=⟨0,1,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩,\,∇f=⟨0,0,-1⟩,
$$

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(4,1,4).$"] ["question-2c76b758-88c8-5667-93d2-dbb6a9e1da40" :question/worked-solution "We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ z & \sqrt{x} & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =[0(0)-(-1)(\sqrt{x})]i-[0(0)-(-1)(z)]j+[0(\sqrt{x})-0(z)]k \\  & =\sqrt{x}\,i-z\,j+0\,k \\  & =⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =(-z)⟨0,1,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩+⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-z,-\frac{z}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩+⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{x},-2z,-\frac{z}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F)(4,1,4) & =⟨\sqrt{4},-2(4),-\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4}}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-8,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2c76b758-88c8-5667-93d2-dbb6a9e1da40" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-cee411fe-3c0d-5c7d-9c42-5d9b1df29d7b" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
79 \div 6
$$

We proceed using long division as usual, continuing until a repeating pattern of digits appears after the decimal point:

![](images/3c/3c9add129b16a1dedeb68e0397f6345d7f481f3bbfdd54c0a35067abaaa15263.svg)

We could continue the division, but the same digit keeps repeating. Thus, the decimal continues with repeating $6$'s:

$$
13.16\ldots
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{79}{6} = 13.16\ldots = 13.1\overline{6}.
$$"] ["knowledge-point-2ee93f86-38d1-591a-b694-a4f455240d75" :knowledge-point/canonical-example "question-2953724f-e9c5-5a58-a253-c1d894297cc0"] ["knowledge-point-4c28dcab-dd12-58c2-88c6-0301dc0f9ce4" :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4c28dcab-dd12-58c2-88c6-0301dc0f9ce4"] [17592186408188 :topic/knowledge-points "knowledge-point-4c28dcab-dd12-58c2-88c6-0301dc0f9ce4"] ["question-975545b6-bff4-5fab-aaf4-e8ee01507788" :question/id #uuid "975545b6-bff4-5fab-aaf4-e8ee01507788"] ["question-975545b6-bff4-5fab-aaf4-e8ee01507788" :question/math-academy-id "e-22727"] ["question-975545b6-bff4-5fab-aaf4-e8ee01507788" :question/problem "Which of the following numbers are rational?

I. $1.577$

II. $8.163452 \ldots$

III. $2.\overline{73}$"] ["question-975545b6-bff4-5fab-aaf4-e8ee01507788" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of our numbers in turn.

- $1.577$ is a rational number because it can be expressed as a ratio of two integers:

$$
1.577 = \dfrac{1\,577}{1\,000}
$$

- $8.163452 \ldots$ is not a rational number. The notation "$\ldots$" tells us that digits after the decimal point extend forever. Because there is no indicated repeating pattern, this represents a non-terminating, non-repeating decimal.

- $2.\overline{73}$ is a rational number. The notation $\overline{73}$ tells us that the digits $7$ and $3$ after the decimal point repeat indefinitely.

$$
2.\overline{73} = 2.73737373\ldots
$$

Any decimal with repeating digits can be represented as a ratio of two integers. In this case,

$$
2.\overline{73}  = \dfrac{271}{99}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""] ["knowledge-point-4c28dcab-dd12-58c2-88c6-0301dc0f9ce4" :knowledge-point/canonical-example "question-975545b6-bff4-5fab-aaf4-e8ee01507788"] ["question-ee55fb2d-2168-5fe7-9d4c-8b219d79c6ed" :question/id #uuid "ee55fb2d-2168-5fe7-9d4c-8b219d79c6ed"] ["question-ee55fb2d-2168-5fe7-9d4c-8b219d79c6ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-357330"] ["question-ee55fb2d-2168-5fe7-9d4c-8b219d79c6ed" :question/problem "Convert $\frac{17}{8}$ into a decimal using long division."] ["question-ee55fb2d-2168-5fe7-9d4c-8b219d79c6ed" :question/worked-solution "To write down the given fraction as a decimal, we need to divide the numerator by the denominator:

["question-5f502aa5-65d4-518a-a479-69aa4507aee1" :question/problem "Which of the following numbers are rational?

I. $1.353124…$

II. $1.5\overset{―}{21}$

III. $4.055$"] ["question-5f502aa5-65d4-518a-a479-69aa4507aee1" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of our numbers in turn.

- $1.353124…$ is not a rational number. The notation "$…$" tells us that digits after the decimal point extend forever. However, there are no repeating digits.

- $1.5\overset{―}{21}$ is a rational number. The notation $\overset{―}{21}$ tells us that the digits $2$ and $1$ after the decimal point repeat indefinitely.

$$
1.5\overset{―}{21}=1.52121212121…
$$

Any decimal with repeating digits can be represented as a ratio of two integers. In this case,

$$
1.5\overset{―}{21}=\frac{1\,506}{990}.
$$

- $4.055$ is a rational number because it can be expressed as a ratio of two integers:

$$
4.055=\frac{4\,055}{1\,000}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] ["question-5f502aa5-65d4-518a-a479-69aa4507aee1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["knowledge-point-4c28dcab-dd12-58c2-88c6-0301dc0f9ce4" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Rational Decimals"] [17592186152676 :question/problem "Which of the following numbers are rational?

I. $3.624$

II. $0.\overset{―}{25}$

III. $7.526380…$"] [17592186152676 :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of our numbers in turn.

- $3.624$ is a rational number because it can be expressed as a ratio of two integers:

$$
3.624=\frac{3\,624}{1\,000}
$$

- $0.\overset{―}{25}$ is a rational number. The notation $\overset{―}{25}$ tells us that the digits $2$ and $5$ after the decimal point repeat indefinitely.

$$
0.\overset{―}{25}=0.2525252525…
$$

Any decimal with repeating digits can be represented as a ratio of two integers. In this case,

$$
0.\overset{―}{25}=\frac{25}{99}.
$$

- $7.526380…$ is not a rational number. The notation "$…$" tells us that digits after the decimal point extend forever. However, there are no repeating digits.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""] [17592186152676 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186150563 :answer-field/correct 17592186150566] ["knowledge-point-4c28dcab-dd12-58c2-88c6-0301dc0f9ce4" :knowledge-point/questions 17592186152676] ["tutorial-6c539020-aca7-5b8f-a2b0-b72c56336242" :tutorial/id #uuid "6c539020-aca7-5b8f-a2b0-b72c56336242"] ["tutorial-6c539020-aca7-5b8f-a2b0-b72c56336242" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15179] ["tutorial-6c539020-aca7-5b8f-a2b0-b72c56336242" :tutorial/title "Introduction"] ["tutorial-6c539020-aca7-5b8f-a2b0-b72c56336242" :tutorial/content "A rational number can have a decimal representation that either *ends* or *repeats*.

In this lesson, we will see how to convert rational numbers written as fractions into decimals using *long division*. 
We begin with examples where the decimal terminates. 

Let's convert $\dfrac{7}{2}$ into a decimal using long division.

To write the fraction as a decimal, we divide the numerator by the denominator:

$$
7 \div 2
$$

We proceed using long division as usual, stopping once we obtain a remainder of $0\mathbin{:}$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{7}{2} = 3.5.
$$"] ["tutorial-b877953a-1821-5fae-aebf-3ff936971679" :tutorial/id #uuid "b877953a-1821-5fae-aebf-3ff936971679"] ["tutorial-b877953a-1821-5fae-aebf-3ff936971679" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15177] ["tutorial-b877953a-1821-5fae-aebf-3ff936971679" :tutorial/title "Repeating Decimals"] ["tutorial-b877953a-1821-5fae-aebf-3ff936971679" :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following rational number:

Notice that, in this case,

$$

$$

This is an example of a **repeating decimal** - a decimal in which the digits after the decimal point continue forever in a *repeating pattern*."] ["tutorial-8545445f-23ee-5309-8571-5a1f6a4b253d" :tutorial/id #uuid "8545445f-23ee-5309-8571-5a1f6a4b253d"] ["tutorial-8545445f-23ee-5309-8571-5a1f6a4b253d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15180] ["tutorial-8545445f-23ee-5309-8571-5a1f6a4b253d" :tutorial/title "Notations for Repeating Decimals"] ["tutorial-8545445f-23ee-5309-8571-5a1f6a4b253d" :tutorial/content "It's convenient to use the following special **bar-notation** to indicate decimals that repeat indefinitely:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}0.\overset{―}{78} & =0.78\,78\,78\,78… \\ 0.\overset{―}{675} & =0.675\,675\,675…\end{aligned}

$$

["question-9d2fd7c0-6fec-5b30-98fe-3b0bf10ba9a4" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,4,4).$"] ["question-9d2fd7c0-6fec-5b30-98fe-3b0bf10ba9a4" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,4,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(2,4,4)=\frac{1}{6}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =-\frac{x}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(2,4,4)=-\frac{2}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{108}, \\ {f}_{y} & =-\frac{y}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}, \\ {f}_{z} & =-\frac{z}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(2,4,4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,4,4) & =⟨{f}_{x}(2,4,4),{f}_{y}(2,4,4),{f}_{z}(2,4,4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{108}(x-2)-\frac{1}{54}(y-4)-\frac{1}{54}(z-4) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{x}{108}+\frac{1}{54}-\frac{y}{54}+\frac{4}{54}-\frac{z}{54}+\frac{4}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x}{108}-\frac{y}{54}-\frac{z}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-9d2fd7c0-6fec-5b30-98fe-3b0bf10ba9a4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-c5948ebf-b36f-50ef-996a-235488992a7d" :answer-field/id #uuid approximation of $f$ at the point $(-2,-3).$"] ["question-4a523061-b982-5542-a530-946bca7d0e33" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-2,-3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,y+3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-2,-3)=-19.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={y}^{2}\, &  & ⇒\,{f}_{x}(-2,-3)=(-3)^{2}=9, \\ {f}_{y} & =2xy &  & ⇒\,{f}_{y}(-2,-3)=2(-2)(-3)=12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-2,-3)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-2,-3) & =⟨9,12⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇\,f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+⟨9,12⟩\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+9(x+2)+12(y+3) \\  & =35+9x+12y.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-4a523061-b982-5542-a530-946bca7d0e33" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-dbb4d8a0-1307-529a-b016-d7f1bd8d71e7" :answer-field/id #uuid {(-5)}^{2})÷({(-2)}^{5}-(-20)).$"] ["question-50989de1-e6f3-5831-87a9-51e32375a2a1" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

First, we consider the expressions inside each of the parentheses. The first one is.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}\times {(-5)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying PEMDAS to this expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}\times {(-5)}^{2} & = \\ \frac{2}{5}\times 25 & = \\ \frac{2}{5}\times \frac{25}{1} & = \\ \frac{2\times 25}{5\times 1} & = \\ \frac{50}{5} & = \\ 10\end{aligned}
$$

The expression inside the second parentheses is.

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-2)}^{5}-(-20).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying PEMDAS to this expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-2)}^{5}-(-20) & = \\ (-32)+20 & = \\ -12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{2}{5}\times {(-5)}^{2})÷({(-2)}^{5}-(-20)) & = \\ 10÷(-12) & = \\ \frac{10}{(-12)} & = \\ -\frac{10}{12} & = \\ -\frac{5}{6}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-50989de1-e6f3-5831-87a9-51e32375a2a1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-eb165dbd-4e64-57b9-b591-6886c0a643cc" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Evaluate $(-3)\times ((-8)^{2}\times \frac{3}{64}).$"] ["question-4b607318-28df-51c2-9737-62f37f3092a8" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

First, consider the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-8)^{2}\times \frac{3}{64}\end{aligned}
$$

Applying PEMDAS to this expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-8)^{2}\times \frac{3}{64} & = \\ 64\times \frac{3}{64} & = \\ \frac{64}{1}\times \frac{3}{64} & = \\ \frac{64\times 3}{1\times 64} & = \\ \frac{\cancel{64}\times 3}{1\times \cancel{64}} & = \\ 3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)\times ((-8)^{2}\times \frac{3}{64}) & = \\ (-3)\times 3 & = \\ -9\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-4b607318-28df-51c2-9737-62f37f3092a8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-82dc6c2e-5b62-5fbc-aec5-c5800d42bb69" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-dff097a9-6d33-544e-9f71-468162e0a004" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

We begin by performing the operations inside the parentheses. So, first we add $(-2)$ to $7$:

$$
\begin{aligned}3+(-2+7)^{2} & =3+{5}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we compute the exponent:

$$

$$"] [17592186179913 :question/answer-fields 17592186177147] [17592186180096 :question/answer-fields 17592186178245] [17592186180703 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to calculate a particle's velocity and displacement when its acceleration is a function of *displacement.* In this lesson, we'll use this knowledge to compute various properties of a particle in motion.

Suppose a particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. Its displacement from the origin is $x\,\rm{m},$ its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ and its acceleration is $2x\,\rm{m/s}^2.$

![](images/52/5222b12a7f08a33dc981ac95bd717cce945e1d2e3565fb3631f108fd0f307a12.png)

Furthermore, suppose $P$ has velocity $2\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $\sqrt{3}\,\rm{m}.$

Let's use this information to determine at which values of $x$ the particle is instantaneously at rest.

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $2x\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =2x.$$

Using the fact that $$\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),$$ we can rewrite our equation as

$$\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x.$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x = \int 2x \:\textrm{d}x$$

which gives the general solution

$$\dfrac12v^2 = x^2+ C.$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=\sqrt 3\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =(\sqrt{3})^{2}+C \\ 2 & =3+C \\ C & =-1\end{aligned}$$

Therefore,

$$\dfrac12v^2 = x^2-1.$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x) = 0\,\rm{m/s}.$ We find the displacement of the particle when $P$ is instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x{:}$

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\,m\end{aligned}$$"] [17592186371070 :question/problem "The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ ${a}_{3},$ and ${a}_{4}$ are given below. $$"] [17592186371070 :question/worked-solution "We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=2 \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=-4 \\ -9{x}_{1}-8{x}_{3}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$

$$

:tutorial/content "To multiply two-digit decimals, we can use the usual method of removing and replacing the decimal point.\n\nAs an example, let's learn how to compute $0.4 \\times 0.9$. We proceed as follows:\n\n**Step 1.** First, ignore the decimal points and multiply as if both numbers were whole numbers:\n\n$$\n4 \\times 9 = 36\n$$\n\n**Step 2.** Then, insert the decimal point in the result so that number of decimal places is equal to the total number of decimal places in *both factors combined.*\n\nHere, there is $\\color{blue}1$ decimal place in $0.4$ and there is $\\color{blue}1$ decimal place in $0.9$, so their product will have a total of\n\n$$\n{\\color{blue}1} + {\\color{blue}1} = 2\n$$\n\ndecimal places.\n\nWe take our value of $36$ and insert a decimal point to make a number with $2$ decimal places:\n\n$$\n2\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n0.4 \\times 0.9 = 0.36 \\,\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6b36f4a0-7deb-5913-be8e-0317929f793d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8550 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "834ec7ff-c309-55d8-b8c4-51a8a44a519b" :step/math-academy-id 90825 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055917}} {:db/id 17592186055917 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054855 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054461 :question/id #uuid "1105c7d8-178a-598c-bf98-3032e506af4d" :question/math-academy-id "e-13681"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a20a2e6d-b919-5385-932a-83df013f47d6" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050007}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055378} {:db/id 17592186055383}] :knowledge-point/title "Multiplying Decimals Smaller Than One"} :step/id #uuid "e032ff82-cb04-58bb-bd2c-e15b9dde6bed" :step/math-academy-id 90826 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055918}} {:db/id 17592186055918 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056063 :tutorial/content "We can use the same method to multiply decimals even when they are greater than $1$. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $V$.\n\nFirst, we subtract $mC$ from both sides of the equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nE &= mC + \\frac{1}{2}mV \\\\\nE - mC &= mC + \\frac{1}{2}mV - mC \\\\\nE - mC &= \\frac{1}{2}mV\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, we multiply by $2$ to get rid of the fraction:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nE - mC &= \\frac{1}{2}mV \\\\\n2 \\cdot (E - mC) &= 2 \\cdot \\frac{1}{2}mV \\\\\n2(E - mC) &= mV\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we divide by $m$ to get $V$ alone:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n2(E - mC) &= mV \\\\\n(2(E - mC))/(m) &= \\frac{mV}{m} \\\\\n(2(E - mC))/(m) &= V\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThus,\n\n$$\nV = \\dfrac{2(E-mC)}{m}\n$$\n\n**Note:** This result assumes that\n\n$$\nm\\neq 0\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186049734} {:db/id 17592186064568 :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134674 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135049 :tutorial/content "We've already seen how to find the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace in the case when the subspace is defined using an orthogonal basis. In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.\n\nFor example, consider the following vectors:\n![](images/28/28ce7470231775d8889555d0dd9f37ee9215044762a40335bd43578b121486a3.svg)\nHow can we find the orthogonal projection $\\mathbf{x}_S$ of the vector $\\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \\textrm{Span}\\{ \\mathbf{a}_1, \\mathbf{a}_2 \\}?$ Notice that since $\\mathbf a_1\\cdot \\mathbf a_2 \\neq 0,$ the vectors $\\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\\mathbf{a}_2$ are not orthogonal.\n\nAs usual, we would like to write $\\mathbf{x}$ as \n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x} = \\mathbf{x}_S + \\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp},\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \\mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \\mathbf{a}_2 \\in S$ and $\\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp} \\!\\in S^\\perp.$\n\n![](images/3a/3a5576fcaf9e0be6fc14978eb91dcbaceee75cbfddaa537fdb05d34b8e31e2e0.png)\n\nSo, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\\\  & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\\\  & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince $\\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp} \\in S^\\perp,$ that is, $\\mathbf{x}_{S^\\perp} \\perp S,$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{1} \\\\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{2}\\end{aligned}\\,⟹\\,\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\\cdot {a}_{1}=0 \\\\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\\cdot =a[({a}^{T}a)^{-1}{a}^{T}x] \\\\  & =a\\,({a}^{T}a)^{-1}{a}^{T}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's compare the above with the formula that we use when we want to project onto an arbitrary \\:\\textrm{d}x\n$$\n\nwhich gives the general solution\n\n$$\n\\dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x + C.\n$$\n\nNow, since $v=\\sqrt{2}\\,\\rm{m/s}$ when $x=1\\,\\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$
