approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by\n\n$$\nf(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.\n$$\n\nSo, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,1,\\pi )$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(0,1,\\pi )+∇f(0,1,\\pi )\\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z-\\pi ⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(0,1,\\pi )=-1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =y{e}^{xy}\\operatorname{cos}⁡z\\,⇒\\,{f}_{x}(0,1,\\pi )=-1, \\\\ {f}_{y} & =x{e}^{xy}\\operatorname{cos}⁡z\\,⇒\\,{f}_{y}(0,1,\\pi )=0, \\\\ {f}_{z} & =-{e}^{xy}\\operatorname{sin}⁡z\\,⇒\\,{f}_{z}(0,1,\\pi )=0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(0,1,\\pi )$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇f(0,1,\\pi ) & =⟨{f}_{x}(0,1,\\pi ),{f}_{y}(0,1,\\pi ),{f}_{z}(0,1,\\pi )⟩ \\\\  & =⟨-1,0,0⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(0,1,\\pi )+∇f(0,1,\\pi )\\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z-\\pi ⟩ \\\\  & ≈-1+⟨-1,0,0⟩\\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z-\\pi ⟩ \\\\  & ≈-1-x.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186125008 :question/id :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2).$" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by\n\n$$\nf(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.\n$$\n\nSo, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇f(-1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\\cdot ⟨x+1,y-\\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={e}^{y}\\, &  & ⇒\\, & {f}_{x}(-1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2)={e}^{\\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=2, \\\\ {f}_{y} & =x{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\\, & {f}_{y}(-1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-1{e}^{\\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=-2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =⟨2,-2⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇\\,f(-1,\\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\\cdot ⟨x+1,\\,y-\\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\\\  & =-2+⟨2,-2⟩\\cdot ⟨x+1,\\,y-\\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\\\  & =-2+2(x+1)-2(y-\\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\\\  & =2\\operatorname{ln}⁡2+2x-2y.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186404953 :question/id #uuid "f0a65ec3-c24d-50c1-a1d2-f9666a246122" :question/math-academy-id "q-98554"} {:db/id 17592186404960 $(-1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by\n\n$$\nf(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.\n$$\n\nSo, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0)$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,0)=1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =2x{e}^{y}\\, &  & ⇒\\, & {f}_{x}(-1,0)=-2, \\\\ {f}_{y} & ={x}^{2}{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\\, & {f}_{y}(-1,0)=1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,0)$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,0) & =⟨-2,1⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\\\  & ≈1+⟨-2,1⟩\\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\\\  & ≈1-2(x+1)+y \\\\  & ≈-1-2x+y.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186124608 \\\\  & =1+⟨-1,-1,0⟩\\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z+1⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can approximate $f(1.02,0.1,-0.96)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=1.02,$ $y=0.1,$ and $z=-0.96$ as $(a,b),$ then\n\n$$\nf(x,y) \\approx f(a,b) + \\nabla f(a,b)\\cdot \\langle x-a, y-b \\rangle.\n$$\n\nWe can extend this result to higher dimensions. \n\nFor example, if $f(x,y, z)$ is differentiable at the point $(a,b, c),$ then \n\n$$\nf(x,y,z) \\approx f(a,b,c) + \\nabla f(a,b,c)\\cdot \\langle x-a, y-b,z-c \\rangle,\n$$\n\nfor all $(x,y,z)$ that lie in some open neighborhood of $(a,b,c).$\n\nMore generally, if a function $f(\\mathbf x)$ in the variable $\\mathbf x = (x_1, x_2. \\dots, x_n)$ is differentiable at the point $\\mathbf x_0\\in \\Bbb R^n,$ then \n\n$$\nf(\\mathbf x) \\approx f(\\mathbf x_0) +  \\nabla f(\\mathbf x_0) \\cdot (\\mathbf x-\\mathbf x_0)\n$$\n\nfor all $\\mathbf x$ that lie in some open neighborhood of $\\mathbf x_0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid :step/math-academy-id 34419 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125556}} {:db/id 17592186125572 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125853 :tutorial/content "Consider the function $f(x,y)=4-x^2-y^2$ at the point $P(1,1).$ We want to find the best linear approximation to this function, valid in a neighborhood of $P.$\n\nThe partial derivatives of $f$ are given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =-2x\\, & ⟹\\, &  & {f}_{x}(1,1)=-2 \\\\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =-2y\\, & ⟹\\, &  & {f}_{y}(1,1)=-2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe partial derivatives are continuous functions at every point, which means that $f$ is differentiable everywhere, and\n\n$$\n\\nabla f (1,1) = \\langle -2, -2\\rangle.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the best linear approximation of $f$ in a neighborhood of $(1,1)$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(1,1)+∇f(1,1)\\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\\\  & =2+⟨-2,-2⟩\\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\\\  & =2+(-2)\\cdot (x-1)+(-2)\\cdot (y-1) \\\\  & =2-2x+2-2y+2 \\\\  & =6-2x-2y.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's take a look at the diagram below. Notice that in the neighborhood of $(x,y)=(1,1)$, the surface and its tangent plane approximation are very close.\n\n![](images/20/20f06226ec7c21583e56249ea2fe5c65c6127cef8a6e05ee4b1d7521ce49dc38.png)\n\n   \n\nTherefore, we can use this to approximate values of $f(x,y)$ that are close to $(1,1).$ For example, using our approximation, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(1.01,1.01) & ≈6-2(1.01)-2(1.01) \\\\  & =1.96.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe actual value of $f$ at this point is $1.9598,$ so our approximation is pretty good!" :tutorial/id #uuid "eb2571f8-ee0b-571d-bacf-34a1e469da8a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5593 :tutorial/title "Linearizing a Quadratic Function"} :step/id #uuid :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)={x}^{2}{e}^{y}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by\n\n$$\nf(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.\n$$\n\nSo, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0)$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,0)=1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =2x{e}^{y}\\, &  & ⇒\\, & {f}_{x}(-1,0)=-2, \\\\ {f}_{y} & ={x}^{2}{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\\, & {f}_{y}(-1,0)=1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,0)$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,0) & =⟨-2,1⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\\\  & ≈1+⟨-2,1⟩\\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\\\  & ≈1-2(x+1)+y \\\\  & ≈-1-2x+y.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "428b58fe-7d44-5904-bbbf-8158fe8c3758"} {:db/id 17592186420933 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125007 ⟨x+1,y⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,0)=1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =2x{e}^{y}\\, &  & ⇒\\, & {f}_{x}(-1,0)=-2, \\\\ {f}_{y} & ={x}^{2}{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\\, & {f}_{y}(-1,0)=1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,0)$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,0) & =⟨-2,1⟩.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\\\  & ≈1+⟨-2,1⟩\\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\\\  & ≈1-2(x+1)+y \\\\  & ≈-1-2x+y.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "428b58fe-7d44-5904-bbbf-8158fe8c3758"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.\nThis course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.\nOn completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.\nStudents then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.\nAs part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.\nStudents will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.\nThe course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.\nA solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.\nStudents also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.\nStudents work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.\nOn the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.\nStudents extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.\nThe course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning methods." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1012 145 Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.\nStudents then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.\nThe course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.\nThe course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.\nStudents then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.\nThe final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. "Let's explore the supremum and infimum of intervals, starting with a closed interval.\n\n**Example A:** $A = [0, 1].$\n\n**Observation (Min/Max):**\nRecall that if a set has a minimum and maximum, they correspond to the infimum and supremum.\nSince $0$ and $1$ are bounds contained in $A,$ we have $\\min(A)=0$ and $\\max(A)=1.$ Thus, we expect:\n\n$$\n\\inf (A) = 0, \\qquad \\sup (A) = 1.\n$$\n\n**Derivation using Sets of Bounds:**\nTo deepen our understanding, we verify this by finding the sets of lower and upper bounds ($L_A$ and $U_A$).\n\n1\\. **Infimum:** We identify $L_A$ and find its maximum.\n\n  - Any number $x \\leq 0$ is a lower bound for $A.$\n\n  - Any number $x > 0$ is *not* a lower bound. Since $0 \\in A$ and $0 < x,$ the number $x$ fails to be a lower bound.\n\n  Therefore, $L_A = (-\\infty, 0]$ and $\\inf (A) = \\max (-\\infty, 0] = \\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0}.$\n\n2\\. **Supremum:** We identify $U_A$ and find its minimum.\n\n  - Any number $x \\geq 1$ is an upper bound for $A.$\n\n  - Any number $x < 1$ is *not* an upper bound. Since $1 \\in A$ and $1 > x,$ the number $x$ fails to be an upper bound.\n\n  Therefore, $U_A = [1, \\infty)$ and $\\sup (A) = \\min [1, \\infty) = \\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}.$" 17592186045417] [17592186163200 1065 10841 17592186045417] [17592186163200 1066 #uuid "46a24733-634e-584e-8d69-01df206cfe24" 17592186045417] [17592186163200 1067 "Supremum and Infimum of a Closed Interval" 17592186045417] [17592186163201 1064 "Consider the following set.\n\n$$\nA = \\left\\{ \\left(\\dfrac 12\\right)^n \\: : \\: n\\in \\mathbb N \\right\\}\n$$\n\nThe elements of $A$ are the terms of the sequence $a_n,$ given by\n\n$$\na_n =\\left(\\dfrac 12\\right)^n, \\qquad n \\in \\mathbb N = \\{1,2,3,4,\\ldots\\}.\n$$\n\nLet's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:\n\n![](images/b2/b2fc98fed45efbeb0ba7a1bfefe61d2f5698ab36b6c026bf5590b63d2da0a38a.png)\n\nNotice that $a_n$ is a decreasing sequence. Therefore, the first term $a_1$ is the maximum of the set. Since $A$ has a maximum, the supremum equals the maximum:\n\n$$\n\\sup(A) = \\max(A) = a_1 = \\dfrac 12\n$$\n\nNow, our set doesn't have a minimum: the points of the sequence get closer and closer to $0$ without reaching it. Let's find the infimum by determining the set of the lower bounds.\n\nNotice that:\n\n- any number $x \\leq 0$ is a lower bound of $A,$\n\n- any number $x > 0$ is **not** a lower bound of $A.$ In other words, we can always find a sufficiently large $n$ so that $\\left(\\dfrac 12\\right)^n$ is smaller than $x$ for any $x > 0.$\n\nTherefore, $(-\\infty, 0]$ is the set of lower bounds of $A,$ and \n\n$$\n\\inf(A) = \\max \\big({-\\infty}, 0\\big] = 0.\n$$" 17592186045417] [17592186163201 1065 10842 17592186045417] [17592186163201 1066 #uuid "90180d58-a7d9-562b-91a3-cccac21bfc91" 17592186045417] [17592186163201 1067 "Sequences" 17592186045417] [17592186163202 1064 "The concepts of supremum and infimum can be extended to functions.\n\nGiven a function $y=f(x),$ the **supremum** and the **infimum** of $f$ are, respectively, the supremum and the infimum of the range of $f.$\n\nThe **supremum** and **infimum** of a function will be denoted as\n\n$$\n\\inf_{x\\in D} f(x), \\qquad \\text{and} \\sup_{x\\in D} f(x),\n$$\n\nwhere $D$ is the domain of the function.\n\nFor example, consider the following parabola:\n\n![](images/69/690b179ad127181eeb316fb9ae9c8085fa6aa96c6d4729c88d176a908950e80e.png)\n\nThe range of $f$ is $A = (-\\infty, 0].$\n\nLet's find the infimum and the supremum of $A.$\n\nTo find the infimum, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.\n\nIn our case, $A$ has no lower bounds.
